Hi all,

I'm using the SIMULATE feature in TMB as accessed in R via obj$simulate() to implement a simulator in R package VAST.  In some cases, its helpful to exactly replicate a simulation experiment by passing the same random-number seed; however, I don't see how to do this using the obj$simulate() feature.

Is there any way to pass a random-number seed, either in TMB code when calling SIMULATE or (ideally) by passing a seed to obj$simulate() on the R side?

Thanks
Jim

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jim,

You could look at simulate.glmmTMB() for an example (sorry if it’s more complicated than necessary).
https://github.com/glmmTMB/glmmTMB/blob/master/glmmTMB/R/methods.R#L1057

object$obj$simulate() is just taking it from set.seed() but simulate.glmmTMB() is written so that it can take the seed from either the function call (and later restore the RNG state (R.seed in the example code) that was in the environment before calling simulate.glmmTMB()), or take the seed from the environment. E.g. s2 and s3 give the same numbers in the example below, but the call to s3 maintains the RNG state that was already in the environment.

data(cbpp, package="lme4")
(bovine <- glmmTMB(cbind(incidence, size-incidence) ~ period + (1|herd),
   family=binomial, data=cbpp))

set.seed(111); s2 <- simulate(bovine)
s3 <- simulate(bovine, seed=111)

Cheers,
Mollie

Hi John

This winter, I switched over to first Linux Mint and then LMDE4 from Win10 (now using the latter). I spent a fair bit of time figuring out the R and TMB installation process for these OSs. I installed R from source, ensuring that all the dependencies were met. For the Ubuntu installation (Linus Mint), here are the steps that I followed (similar for LMDE4 except for the repository):

Add following line to end of .bashrc file in the home directory
            export PATH=~/:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/local/games:/usr/games:/usr/local/ sbin:/usr/sbin:/sbin   # need to make sure that the binaries can be found

Download Source tarfile (https://cran.r-project.org/) and put into R-3.6.3 (version I installed) subdirectory under home directory (~) and extract all files. Installation of many files will ultimately be in this directory; Instructions in README and INSTALL files

Check that following tools are installed (LM Software Manager)
G++
Build-Essential
G Fortran
Default-Jdk

In Software Sources utility, add repositories
Turn on Source Code repository toggle
To Additional Repositories, add
deb https://cloud.r-project.org/bin/linux/ubuntu bionic-cran35/
In Software Sources utility, enter fingerprint to public key in Download tab
E298A3A825C0D65DFD57CBB651716619E084DAB9
sudo apt update                                                                                                    # make sure that all packages are up to date; might need to execute sudo apt upgrade
sudo apt build-dep r-base > output_builddeprbase                                               # installs all dependencies for r-base (requires URI in Sources.list.d directory) & if desired stores output in output_builddeprbase
./configure –enable-R-shlib &> output_configure to create a Makefile    # will install binaries in usr/local/bin
make &> output_make
make check &> output_makecheck                                                                       # does some checks of the installation; not essential but good to do
sudo make install &> output_makeinstall                                                              # installs software; by default, binaries are installed in the usr/local/bin/<program name> directory unless ./configure option specifies otherwise
sudo R                                                                                                                    # RcppEigen was installed in the usr/local/lib/R/library, so sudo was needed
install.packages(“TMB”, keep_outputs = TRUE)                                                    # saves log of installation in TMB.out file
The Matrix package was installed along with all the others when R was installed with no problem. The details of the above may be different in your case but the overall steps should be the same.

Hope this helps

Bob

messages.body_plain:
Are there any problems with using the effects and emmeans packages to interpret glmmTMB models with Tweedie distributions?

I have glmmTMB models using the Tweedie distribution, and I want to draw inference about the direction and magnitude of the predicted effects. In the model given below:

glmmTMB(Shoot.weight ~ Species + N.Level + Rhiz + Species:N.Level + Species:Rhiz + N.Level:Rhiz + N.Level:Rhiz:Species + (1|Block) + (1|Acc), family=tweedie, data=DcleanSOY)

I have a significant effect of the N.Level:Rhiz:Species interaction term (based on a likelihood ratio test). N level is a continuous predictor, and Rhiz and Species are both two-level factors.I have used the effects package to make a plot with 95% confidence intervals to interpret this 3-way interaction. I have also made separate models for each level of the N level predictor, and used emmeans to get pairwise Tukey contrasts of the Rhiz and Species predictors at each N level.

Can I base my inference on these 95% confidence intervals and/or emmeans contrasts, or are these methods not supported for Tweedie glmmTMB models?

Thanks! -Niall
